title: Morning Digest, Tuesday 27 October 2026
intro: Anthropic files to go public and shows its books, OpenAI says its models have overturned a cornerstone of complexity theory, Israel votes today, and the Speaker weighs his next move after the Centre Party's talks failed.

items.title: Anthropic files for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT
items.body: The S-1 shows 16.3 billion dollars of first-half revenue, fourteen times a year earlier, and an 80.7 billion dollar net loss that is almost entirely a paper charge on convertible notes as its valuation rose; the operating loss was 693 million. The co-founders keep 50.1 percent of the votes.

items.title: OpenAI claims AI-made proofs of three famous open problems
items.body: Its internal models are said to have disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis (that problems like 3-SAT need exponential time, an assumption hundreds of results rest on), proved local smoothing in every dimension, which would settle the Kakeya and Stein restriction conjectures, and shown that four-dimensional quantum field theories such as Yang-Mills exist. The first two come with machine-checked Lean proofs; all await independent review, led for ETH by its originators with Ryan Williams and for physics by David Gross.
items.source: The Next Web; Interesting Engineering; Unite.AI, 26 Oct

items.title: Israel votes today
items.body: Polls close at 21:00 Stockholm time, with exit polls straight after; final surveys put Eisenkot's Yashar slightly ahead of Likud and both blocs short of 61 seats. Reports that security chiefs backed a pre-election strike on Iran were denied by the defence minister.

items.title: Oil falls 6 percent as mediators converge on Tehran
items.body: Brent dropped from about 117 to about 110 dollars a barrel after Qatari mediators, coordinating with Washington, reached Tehran and Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish security chiefs followed. Trump framed his choice as a deal or 'finishing them off'; before the war Brent traded near 72 dollars.

items.title: Washington floats Orbán as next UN secretary-general
items.body: The Wall Street Journal reports that Trump officials back the former Hungarian prime minister, who lost power in April, possibly as a joint US-Russian-Chinese candidate; nothing is decided and Poland says it would not support him. Guterres's term ends on 31 December.

items.title: Kyiv wants peace talks brought forward
items.body: Ukraine is pushing to start the US-brokered three-way talks in Abu Dhabi at least a week earlier than the mid-November date Moscow named, citing winter power cuts; Russia has not agreed.

items.title: Government formation: the centrist attempt fails, and the Speaker's next step is open
items.body: Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist handed back her exploratory mandate on Monday, saying there is a majority for centrist policies but not for a centrist government; KD and the Liberals still back Ulf Kristersson, and C still refuses the Left Party in government. Andreas Norlén will consult the parties by phone before deciding. He has three prime-ministerial votes left before a snap election, commentators expect Kristersson to be asked next, and Kristersson called the outcome logical. The 2027 budget is due by 12 November.
items.source: The Local; SVT live blog, 26 Oct

items.title: Far more children in gang violence than thought
items.body: Socialstyrelsen found that 264 children and young people were prosecuted or tried for serious gang-linked violence in 2020-2024, about one in ten under 15, against an earlier estimate of 150-200; it will now study every case.

items.title: Scheduled
bullets: Tuesday 27 October: Israel votes; exit polls at 21:00 Stockholm time. Speaker Norlén may announce his next step in government formation this week.
Wednesday 28 October: US Federal Reserve decision and Kevin Warsh's press conference, with a hold widely expected; Microsoft and Alphabet report after the US close.
Thursday 29 October: ECB rate decision; first US estimate of third-quarter GDP; Amazon and Intel report; Serbia's final election results are due around now.
Early November: Ukraine-Russia-US talks in Abu Dhabi, date not fixed.

items.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Terra
items.body: The mid-tier model, aimed at agents and computer use, costs 1 dollar per million input tokens and 5 per million output, about half the flagship Sol, and early reports say it is roughly three times faster than GPT-5.6 Terra.

items.title: Meta seeks up to 95 billion dollars in new shares for AI
items.body: It is its largest equity raise ever: about 35 billion dollars in offerings now and up to 60 billion sold gradually into the market from early 2027. Meta raised its capital-spending forecast to 135-145 billion dollars after its first quarter of negative free cash flow (cash from operations minus investment) in over a decade.

items.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to about 60,000 staff
items.body: About a quarter of the workforce, at vice-president level and below in the US, Canada, India and the UK, can take a severance package and leave at year-end; data-centre roles are excluded, and the company is under cost pressure from its AI build-out.
items.source: Axios Seattle (Seattle Times); AI Weekly, 26 Oct

items.title: Research pulse
bullets: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy (Google DeepMind): standard implementations round the correct class's gradient to zero once a model is confident enough (a margin of about 16.6 in fp32, 5.5 in bf16) while other gradients survive, which the authors show causes the 'Slingshot' loss spikes seen in grokking; a few lines of rewritten JAX remove the spikes and stop distilled students drifting from their teachers (arXiv 2610.31642).

On-Policy Self-Training (Google, Ulm): a small Gemma model writes its own questions and worked answers from topic names, keeps only those it cannot yet solve reliably, and learns from a copy of itself that sees the answers, lifting MMLU from 37.5 to 47.7 percent without any human-written training data (arXiv 2610.32770).

PhysLadder: a 16-task benchmark with matched simulated and real setups finds GPT-6 Astra, used zero-shot as a robot controller, succeeds 80 percent of the time on simple contact tasks, 48 percent when force must be regulated and never on tasks needing coordinated contact changes, from three trials per task (arXiv 2610.34527).
items.source: alphaXiv hot list; Hugging Face daily papers; arXiv, 22-25 Oct

must_reads.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
must_reads.why: The most-cited paper of the century: skip connections made very deep networks trainable, and they're in every modern architecture.

must_read_backups.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
must_read_backups.why: Cryo-electron microscopy finally captures the fleeting protein ring the malaria parasite uses to push its way into red blood cells, and the team used AI-assisted protein design to build an inhibitor that blocks it in the test tube: a new angle on a disease that kills about 600,000 people a year as drug resistance spreads.

must_read_backups.title: Anthropic S-1 Breakdown
must_read_backups.why: A line-by-line reading of the first financial statements ever published by a frontier AI lab, with every figure linked back to the filing: how compute is contracted 12-18 months ahead and expensed as capacity comes online, why an $80.7 billion half-year loss is mostly a non-cash accounting mark on convertible notes, and what roughly $600 billion in compute agreements and leased data centres mean for the company's cash. Makes the economics of a frontier lab concrete. Prepared from the public filing by a research firm that uses Claude in its product.
